{{Short description|American statistician (1942–2017)}}
{{tone|date=July 2010}}
'''William L. Sanders''' (26 April 1942<ref name="obit">{{cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/tennessean/obituary.aspx?pid=184563925|title=Dr. William "Bill" Sanders|date=18 March 2017|work=The Tennessean|access-date=22 May 2017}}</ref> – 16 March 2017) was an American statistician, a senior research fellow with the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]]. He developed the Tennessee Value-Added Assessment System (TVAAS), also known as the Educational Value-Added Assessment System (EVAAS), a method for measuring a teacher's effect on student performance by tracking the progress of students against themselves over the course of their school career with their assignment to various teachers' classes.

==Life==
Sanders was born in 1942 in [[Shelbyville, Tennessee]] and received a bachelor of science degree in animal science (1964) and a doctorate in statistics and [[quantitative genetics]] (1968) from the [[University of Tennessee]]. From 1972 to 2000, Sanders was a statistical consultant for the [[Institute of Agricultural Research and Development|Institute of Agricultural Research]], which is part of the UT system; he also was an adjunct professor in the school's College of Business. Sanders left the university to join the [[SAS Institute]].<ref name="sas">{{cite web|work=SAS|url=http://blogs.sas.com/content/statelocalgov/2015/06/19/the-man-behind-vam-bill-sanders-honored-for-a-lifetime-of-education-service/|date=19 June 2015|first=Nadja|last=Young|title=The man behind VAM: Bill Sanders honored for a lifetime of education service|access-date=22 May 2017}}</ref>

In 2015, Sanders was awarded the James Bryant Conant Award.{{r|sas}}

He died on 16 March 2017 at the age of 74.<ref name="nyt">{{cite news|work=The New York Times|date=19 May 2017|access-date=22 May 2017|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/05/19/upshot/the-little-known-statistician-who-transformed-education.html?_r=0|title=The Little-Known Statistician Who Taught Us to Measure Teachers|first=Kevin|last=Carey}}</ref>

==Value-added assessment==
Sanders's primary contributions, however, were in education. In 1982, Sanders happened upon a newspaper article about attempts by then-Governor [[Lamar Alexander]] to introduce merit pay for teachers, which raised questions as to the qualifications for merit. He sent a letter to the governor explaining a potential method, and while he did not use it, the idea was revived eight years later by [[Ned McWherter]]. The system depends on calculating expected versus actual growth trajectories for students as scored on standardized exams; these "value-added" scores fell into a [[bell curve]].{{r|nyt}} Tennessee began using the system in 1993, and it since has been adopted by a number of other [[school district]]s across the United States.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cgp.upenn.edu/pdf/Braun-ETS%20Using%20Student%20Progress%20to%20Evaluate%20Teachers.pdf|first=Henry|last=Braun|title=Using Student Progress To Evaluate Teachers: A Primer on Value-Added Models|publisher=ETS|year=2005}}</ref> Sanders' approach has been used to support the theory that the quality of teachers is central to educational achievement.

The [[Pennsylvania]] and [[New Hampshire]] Departments of Education sponsor pilots, and the [[Iowa School Board Association]] sponsors his value-added work in that state. [[Battelle for Kids]] provides interpretation and use trainings for the SAS EVAAS services for the participating districts in Ohio.

"Using mixed model equations, TVAAS uses the [[covariance matrix]] from this multivariate, longitudinal data set to evaluate the impact of the educational system on student progress in comparison to national [[Psychometrics|norm]]s, with data reports at the district, school, and teacher levels."<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://pareonline.net/getvn.asp?v=10&n=11|title=Growth Models in Action: Selected Case Studies|journal=Practical Assessment, Research and Evaluation|volume=10|issue=11|year=2005|first1=Jessica|last1=Goldstein|first2=Peter|last2=Behuniak}}</ref> The model focuses on academic gains rather than raw achievement scores.

===Criticism===
Dr. Ballou, in Lissitz (Ed.), 2005, "Value Added Models in Education: Theory and Applications," analyzed the TVAAS and determined that value added-assessment of teachers are fallible estimates of teacher contribution to student learning, stating that [[standard error (statistics)|standard error]]s of value-added estimates are large. Author thinks that value added models are merely one useful tool that should be used as one of many assessments in a comprehensive system of evaluation.

Researchers from the [[RAND Corporation]] studied Dr. Sanders' method and determined that his approach does not satisfactorily account for bias, cautioning that non-educational effects may be attributed by mistake to teachers, with no way of effectively determining the magnitude of the error.<ref>{{cite web|work=RAND|url=http://www.rand.org/pubs/monographs/MG158.html|title=Evaluating Value-Added Models for Teacher Accountability|author=Daniel F. McCaffrey |author2=Daniel Koretz |author3=J. R. Lockwood |author4=Laura S. Hamilton |date=2004}}</ref> Ballou (2002) and Kupermintz (2003) further support this claim, claiming that non-educational factors have a noticeable impact on the evaluation of teachers despite efforts to account for them in the model.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://harcourtassessment.com/NR/rdonlyres/2C54ADBA-9959-4F82-82B3-8E65FB822088/0/ValueAdded.pdf |title=Contemporary Report<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2007-04-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927063928/http://harcourtassessment.com/NR/rdonlyres/2C54ADBA-9959-4F82-82B3-8E65FB822088/0/ValueAdded.pdf |archive-date=2007-09-27  }}</ref>

The use of merit pay based on VAM has been discredited in articles by [[Daniel H. Pink|Dan Pink]]<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/as-teacher-merit-pay-spreads-one-noted-voice-cries-it-doesnt-work/2012/02/14/gIQAtRpsFR_story.html?socialreader_check=0&denied=1|first=Lyndsey|last=Layton|newspaper=The Washington Post|title=As teacher merit pay spreads, one noted voice cries, 'It doesn't work'|date=15 February 2012|access-date=22 May 2017}}</ref> and more generally as a business practice in the ''Harvard Business Review''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hbr.org/2012/01/tackling-business-problems/ar/1#.TvtyhA4E5ps.twitter|work=Harvard Business Review|title=Stop Tying Pay to Performance|author1=Bruno S. Frey |author2=Margit Osterloh |date=Jan–Feb 2012|access-date=22 May 2017}}</ref> The accuracy of VAM for evaluating individual teachers has been further discredited by the Economic Policy Institute<ref>{{cite journal|title=Problems with the Use of Student Test Scores to Evaluate Teachers|date=29 August 2010|journal=EPI Briefing Paper|author=Eva L. Baker |author2=Paul E. Barton |author3=Linda Darling-Hammond |author4=Edward Haertel |author5=Helen F. Ladd |author6=Robert L. Linn |author7=Diane Ravitch |author8=Richard Rothstein |author9=Richard J. Shavelson |author10=Lorrie A. Shepard |url=https://epi.3cdn.net/b9667271ee6c154195_t9m6iij8k.pdf|access-date=22 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160308004403/http://epi.3cdn.net/b9667271ee6c154195_t9m6iij8k.pdf|archive-date=8 March 2016|df=dmy-all}}</ref> and by mathematician John Ewing.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Notices of the AMS|url=http://www.ams.org/notices/201105/rtx110500667p.pdf|first=John|last=Ewing|title=Mathematical Intimidation: Driven by the Data|date=May 2011|access-date=22 May 2017}}</ref>
